newsitem.title: ITALY: Serbian opposition sees Milosevic out this year.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition sees Milosevic out this year.

text.p: Opposition leader Vuk Draskovic said on Friday he believed Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic would be out of power by the end of the year and urged the West to raise the pressure on him to reinstate annulled elections.

In an interview in Rome, where he and co-leaders of the Zajedno (Together) coalition were meeting Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, Draskovic said Milosevic had lost majority support in Serbia and was acting like a dictator.
"I am quite sure this is the last year of Milosevic's rule in Serbia," Draskovic told Reuters Television.
"Very many people are against Milosevic. The majority of people are against Milosevic," he said.

Zajedno has staged 60 days of protests on the streets of Belgrade to try to force Milosevic and his ruling Socialist Party (SPS) to recognise opposition victories in local elections in the capital and elsewhere in Serbia on November 17.
Their protests are the biggest challenge to the 10-year rule of Milosevic, who called on Thursday for economic reforms in Serbia but maintained his silence on the vote fraud.

The 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said in Vienna on Thursday that Milosevic should stop making piecemeal concessions to the opposition and should respect their victories.

The European Parliament in Strasbourg also passed a resolution saying the European Union and its individual member countries should freeze relations with Serbia until democracy has been established there.
But Draskovic said he was unimpressed by international action so far.
"I am not quite satisified with international pressure because that pressure is not very effective," he said.

He said it was the duty of the major powers which obtained Milosevic's signature to the 1995 Dayton accords that ended the war in Bosnia to make sure he respected the commitments made in the agreement to fostering democracy in the region.

Draskovic said recognition of the November 17 results was the "condition of all conditions". He urged Milosevic's isolation but stopped short of calling for a resumption of international economic sanctions against Serbia.

"Against Milosevic and his Mafia, yes. Not against our state and people because the people are suffering too much. The biggest sanction...against Serbia is Mr Milosevic and his dictatorship," Draskovic said.
Electoral commissions in Belgrade and Nis, Serbia's second city, have ordered the opposition victories restored, but Socialist hardliners say they will challenge this.
Draskovic and Zajedno co-leaders Zoran Djindjic and Vesna Pesic flew to Rome from Belgrade on Thursday night in an official government plane for Friday's meeting with Dini.
It was not clear what concrete action on the Serbian crisis might emerge from the talks, which some diplomats said appeared to amount to a fence-mending exercise by Italy.

Dini claimed credit last month for obtaining an undertaking from Milosevic during talks in Belgrade to allow an OSCE mission led by former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez to visit Serbia and investigate the polls. It found the opposition won.
Dini, however, angered Zajedno during the same visit when he said reinstatement of the disputed election results was not "on the cards" as a basis for dialogue with Milosevic.
